q: 1. In a reinforced concrete T-beam (in which the flange is in compression), the position of neutral axis will
options: depend on the thickness of flange is in relation to total depth and percentage of reinforcement
at the junction of flange and web
explain: The position of the neutral axis is determined by the equilibrium of total compression and total tension, which depends on the steel ratio and the geometry of the section.

q: 2. The width of the flange of T-beam should be less than
options: one-third of the effective span of the T-beam
distance between the centres of T-beam
breadth of the rib plus twelve times the thickness of the slab
explain: The effective width of a T-beam flange is limited to the minimum of several factors (span/6 + bw + 6df, or center-to-center distance) to account for shear lag.

q: 3. The width of the flange of L-beam, should be less than
options: breadth of the rib + four times thickness of the slab
breadth of the rib + half clear distance between ribs
explain: Similar to T-beams, L-beams have specific geometric limits in the code for 'effective width'—usually based on span, rib width, and slab thickness.

q: 4. Thought the effective depth of a T-beam is the distance between the top compression edge to centre of the tensile reinforcement, for heavy loads, it is taken as
explain: For heavy loading conditions in flanged beams, a stiffer section is required, typically leading to an effective depth around 1/12 of the span.

q: 5. For the design of a simply supported T-beam the ratio of the effective span to the overall depth the beam is limited to
explain: For span/depth ratios regarding deflection control (IS 456), the value for a simply supported beam is generally taken as 20.

q: 6. The maximum strain in the tension reinforcement at failure shall not be less than
explain: Per Limit State Method (IS 456), the minimum strain in steel at failure to ensure ductility is (0.87fy / Es) + 0.002. Note: 0.87 is 1/1.15.

q: 7. The ratio of the compressive strength of concrete is structure to the characteristic strength of concrete in cube is equal to
explain: Because of size and shape differences between a test cube and the actual structure, the design compressive strength of concrete in the structure is taken as 0.67 times the cube strength (fck).

q: 8. The shape of the stress-strain curve for compression in concrete is generally taken to be
explain: In the Limit State Method, the stress-strain block is usually assumed to be parabolic up to a strain of 0.002 and rectangular thereafter.

q: 9. The partial factor of safety for steel in limit state design is
explain: The partial safety factor for steel (γs) is 1.15 because steel is a factory-manufactured material with better quality control than concrete.

q: 10. The partial factor of safety for concrete in limit state design is
explain: The partial safety factor for concrete (γc) is 1.50, reflecting higher uncertainty in site-mixed concrete compared to steel.

q: 11. The maximum allowable percentage of tension reinforcement in R.C.C. beams is
explain: To prevent congestion and ensure proper concrete placement, IS 456 limits the maximum area of tension reinforcement to 4% of the gross cross-sectional area.

q: 12. A continuous beam shall be deemed to be a deep beam if the ratio of effective span to overall depth, is
explain: According to IS 456, a beam is considered deep when the L/D ratio is less than 2.0 for a simply supported beam and less than 2.5 for a continuous beam.

q: 13. The maximum area of tension reinforcement in beams shall not exceed
explain: Same as Q240; the limit is 4% of the gross area (bD).

q: 14. A reinforced concrete beam is design to resist
explain: A complete beam design must account for flexural tension (steel), flexural compression (concrete/steel), and shear (stirrups).

q: 15. Concrete is fairly strong in
options: tension but very weak in compression
compression but very weak in tension
explain: Concrete is a brittle material that performs well under compression but has very little tensile strength (roughly 1/10th of its compressive strength).

q: 16. Steel is very strong
explain: While steel can handle both, its primary purpose in RCC is its high tensile strength to compensate for concrete's weakness.

q: 17. In singly reinforced simply supported beams, the reinforced steel bars are placed
options: near the bottom of the beam
near the top of the beam
at the neutral axis of the beam
anywhere in the cross section of the beam
explain: In a simply supported beam, the bottom fiber is in tension, so the reinforcement must be placed there.

q: 18. A reinforced concrete beam subjected to a monotonously increasing load may fail at
explain: A beam design ensures that it only fails when it reaches its ultimate capacity (Ultimate Strength Stage).

q: 19. The simple bending equation is applicable to a reinforced concrete beam subjected to a monotonously increasing load when the beam remains in
explain: Simple bending theory (linear elastic) applies best when the section is homogenous and uncracked. Once cracks appear, the section properties change significantly.

q: 20. At cracked concrete stage of a reinforced concrete beam, the maximum tensile stress in concrete remains
options: less than its modulus of rupture
more than its modulus of rupture
explain: Concrete cracks once the tensile stress exceeds its Modulus of Rupture (flexural tensile strength).

q: 21. The analysis and design of reinforced concrete beam at the cracked concrete stage is done by
explain: The Working Stress Method (WSM) is based on the elastic theory and assumes the concrete is cracked and the steel carries all tension, focusing on serviceability at the cracked stage.

q: 22. The ratio of the depth of the parabolic and rectangular portion block at the limit state of collapse of a singly reinforced section is
explain: In the IS 456 stress block, the rectangular portion is 3/7th and the parabolic portion is 4/7th of the neutral axis depth. The ratio 4/7 : 3/7 is 4:3.

q: 23. The distance between the lines of action of compression and tensile forces in a singly reinforced beam is called
explain: The lever arm (z) is the internal distance between the resultant compressive force (C) in concrete and the resultant tensile force (T) in steel.

q: 24. If the ratio of steel to concrete in a beam is such that maximum strain in both materials reach simultaneously, the beam is referred to as
explain: A balanced section is a theoretical design where the concrete reaches its maximum allowable compressive strain at the exact same time the steel reaches its yield strain.

q: 25. Compression failure of simply reinforced beam occurs in
explain: In an over-reinforced beam, the concrete reaches its crushing strain before the steel yields, leading to a sudden, brittle compression failure.

q: 26. Tension failure occurs is singly reinforced beam in
explain: In an under-reinforced beam, the steel yields first. This provides ample warning (cracking and deflection) before the concrete eventually crushes, termed a tension failure.

q: 27. Yielding of steel in singly reinforced beam occurs in
explain: Yielding of steel is the defining characteristic of an under-reinforced section, ensuring a ductile failure mode.

q: 28. The ratio of the limiting value of the depth of neutral axis and the depth of the section of a singly reinforced beam is equal to
explain: This formula is derived from the linear strain diagram where the maximum concrete strain is 0.0035 and the minimum steel strain is 0.002 + 0.87fy/Es.

q: 29. The limiting moment of resistance for a singly reinforced beam using Fe 250 steel and general grade concrete, is
explain: For Fe 250 steel (mild steel), the limiting moment of resistance factor (Mu,lim) is 0.148 (rounded to 0.149 in some texts) times fck·bd².

q: 30. The most economical design of singly reinforced beams is given by
explain: Limit State Method (LSM) is more economical as it uses partial safety factors and accounts for the non-linear behavior of concrete, allowing for smaller sections than WSM.

q: 31. To ensure that under the applied moment the concrete and steel in singly reinforced beam reach their stresses, the minimum area of steel
explain: As per IS 456, the minimum tension reinforcement (As) is given by As/bd = 0.85/fy.

q: 32. For a rectangular simply supported beam for 4.5 m effective span, based on the code restriction, the depth is
explain: For a simply supported beam, span/depth = 20. Thus, Depth = 4500 / 20 = 225 mm.

q: 33. The strain at the level of compression reinforcement is doubly reinforced beam is
explain: From the strain triangle, the strain at depth d' is linearly proportional to the distance from the neutral axis: εsc = 0.0035 * (xu - d') / xu.

q: 34. In doubly reinforced beams, the percentage of the maximum compression reinforcement of the gross cross-sectional area of beam should not exceed
explain: Similar to tension reinforcement, compression reinforcement is also capped at 4% of the gross area to prevent congestion.

q: 35. For simply supported beams of spans above 10 m, span to depth ratio 20 must be multiplied to get permitted value by
explain: For spans exceeding 10m, the span-to-depth ratios are modified by multiplying by (10 / span in meters).

q: 36. When strains in compression zone of the concrete of a loaded singly reinforced beam, cause crushing of concrete, the failure is known as
explain: Primary compression failure occurs in over-reinforced sections where concrete reaches its limit before the steel yields.

q: 37. The capacity of beam is determined by the load which causes
explain: In standard under-reinforced design, the beam's capacity is reached when the steel yields (ultimate limit state).

q: 38. For design purpose of flexural members, the compressive strength of concrete is assumed to be
explain: Design strength = (0.67 * fck) / 1.5 (Partial Safety Factor) ≈ 0.446 fck, often simplified or rounded to 0.42-0.45 in various literature batches.

q: 39. For the design of flexural members, the safety partial fact for compressive strength
explain: The partial safety factor for concrete (γc) is 1.5.

q: 40. For the design purpose of flexural members, the partial safety factor for stress in the reinforcement
explain: The partial safety factor for steel (γs) is 1.15.

q: 41. A double reinforced beam may be provided from
explain: Doubly reinforced beams are used when depth is limited (headroom/architecture) or to increase ductility and resist reversal of moments (structural).

q: 42. The maximum diameter of the reinforcement bars in R.C.C. beams is limited to
options: one-eighth of the least dimension of the beams
one-tenth of the depth of beams
explain: General detailing guidelines suggest bar diameter should not exceed 1/8th of the least dimension to ensure bond and concrete flow.

q: 43. The maximum spacing of the torsional reinforcement in R.C.C. beams must not exceed
explain: Torsional stirrups must be closely spaced; the limit is the least of x1, (x1+y1)/4, or 300mm.

q: 44. The probability that the actual strengths of material is more than or equal to its characteristic strength is
explain: Characteristic strength is defined as the value below which not more than 5% of test results are expected to fall, meaning 95% are above it.

q: 45. For simply supported slabs spanning in one direction, the ratio of span to overall depth should exceed
explain: For slabs, the span/overall depth ratio is typically kept around 25-30 for simply supported spans to control deflection.

q: 46. For cantilever beams and slabs, the basic value of span to effective depth ratio is
explain: The code provides basic L/d ratios for deflection control: 7 for cantilevers, 20 for simply supported, and 26 for continuous.

q: 47. For the simply supported beams and slabs the basic value of span to effective depth ratio is
explain: As per IS 456, the basic span-to-effective-depth ratio for simply supported members is 20.

q: 48. The minimum factor of safety against overturning for a retaining wall is
explain: Stability requirements dictate a minimum factor of safety of 2.0 against overturning to account for soil variations.

q: 49. The minimum factor of safety against sliding for a retaining wall is
explain: The minimum factor of safety against sliding is 1.5, often increased if soil conditions are poor.

q: 50. Reinforcement is normally used in cast-in-situ concrete to
explain: Even if the member doesn't carry external tension, reinforcement is necessary to control cracking caused by temperature and shrinkage.
